summary: This document specifies integrity and replay protection for the MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) and OLSRv2. It uses an HMAC-SHA-256 Integrity Check Value TLV and a Timestamp TLV.

eli5.summary: Neighbors in a wireless group can be tricked by fake or repeated notes. This adds a tamper seal and time stamp so cheats are caught.

questions: what is an integrity check value tlv
how does olsrv2 prevent replay attacks
subtitle: A required tamper seal and freshness stamp for the control messages of wireless mesh routing protocols.

tldr.problem: NHDP and OLSRv2 let routers in a mobile ad hoc network (MANET) learn about neighbors and links, but an attacker could forge messages, lie about links or replay old messages.
tldr.mechanism: Each message carries an Integrity Check Value TLV computed with HMAC-SHA-256 and a Timestamp TLV based on POSIX time. Receivers reject messages with a missing or bad ICV, or with a timestamp that is too old.
tldr.outcome: Implementations of NHDP and OLSRv2 must include the mechanism, and deployments should use it. It does not distribute keys or catch compromised routers that hold valid keys.

today: RFC 7183 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6130 and RFC 7181. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why NHDP and OLSRv2 Need Protection
sections.content:
RFC 7183 updates RFC 6130 (NHDP, the neighborhood discovery protocol) and RFC 7181 (OLSRv2, a link state routing protocol) by defining security mechanisms that implementations must include: integrity protection and replay protection.

Both use the TLV mechanism of RFC 5444 to add information to control messages. The ICV and TIMESTAMP TLVs themselves are defined in RFC 7182. A deployment may choose alternatives, or no protection at all, but the RFC says using none is not recommended.

The mechanism sits between RFC 5444 packet parsing and generation and the NHDP or OLSRv2 message processing. Messages that fail the check are dropped before the routing protocols see them.
sections.eli5: The routers need a way to know a message is real and fresh. This adds a seal and a time stamp to every message before it goes out and checks them when it arrives.

sections.title: Applicability and What Is Left Out
sections.content:
Implementations of RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 MUST include this mechanism, and deployments SHOULD use it unless a different security mechanism is more appropriate. A router able to generate correct integrity check values is considered trusted.

The RFC is explicit about what it does not do. It does not say which key identifiers to use when routers share more than one secret key, does not distribute the shared keys, and does not detect or revoke compromised routers that hold valid keys.

Because a message without a valid ICV is rejected, routers that lack this mechanism are ignored by routers that use it. By design the two groups form disjoint MANETs.
sections.eli5: It says who must use the seal and also admits what it cannot do, like handing out the secret stamp or spotting a teammate who has turned bad.

sections.title: TLVs Added to Each Message
sections.content:
A conforming message must carry at least one ICV Message TLV and at least one TIMESTAMP Message TLV. Implementations must support this version of the ICV TLV: type extension 1 for TC messages or 2 for HELLO messages, with hash-function 3 (SHA-256) and cryptographic-function 3 (HMAC). The TIMESTAMP TLV uses type extension 1.

The ICV value may be truncated as specified in RFC 7182, and the length may be set by configuration. A message may carry several ICV TLVs, provided each uses a different key or algorithm.

HELLO messages use a different ICV type extension from TC messages because the HELLO ICV also covers the source address of the IP datagram carrying it. NHDP uses that address to identify a neighbor interface. A TC message is forwarded in a new packet, so it has no single source address.
sections.eli5: Every message gets two extra labels: a secret seal and a clock reading. Different kinds of messages use slightly different seals.

sections.title: Generating and Checking Messages
sections.content:
After a message is generated and before it is sent, the sender temporarily removes any existing ICV TLVs and sets msg-hop-count and msg-hop-limit, if present, to 0. It then adds the TIMESTAMP TLV and then the ICV TLV, restores the removed ICV TLVs and puts the hop fields back. All TIMESTAMP TLVs must be inserted before ICV TLVs are added.

On receipt, a message is invalid for processing if it lacks exactly one TIMESTAMP TLV of the selected version, lacks exactly one ICV TLV using the selected algorithm and key identifier, or if either fails validation.

To validate the ICV, the receiver removes all ICV TLVs, zeroes the hop fields, recomputes the ICV and compares it with the received value, truncating its own result first if the received one was truncated. For the timestamp (type extension 1), validation fails if the current POSIX time minus the timestamp is greater than the maximum allowed difference.
sections.eli5: The sender stamps the message the same way every time, and the receiver redoes the stamp. If the two stamps differ, or the clock reading is too old, the message is binned.

sections.title: Timestamp Age Limits
sections.content:
Two router parameters set how old a message may be: MAX_HELLO_TIMESTAMP_DIFF for HELLO messages (used by NHDP) and MAX_TC_TIMESTAMP_DIFF for TC messages (used by OLSRv2). Each must be greater than 0 and a message older than the limit is silently discarded.

Both must be at least as large as the maximum expected age of a message. A HELLO travels one hop, but a TC message may be forwarded many times, and jitter adds up to F_MAXJITTER per hop except the last. Link-layer delay and the time spent processing ICVs also count. The values may be raised to allow for clock differences, but values that are too large defeat the purpose.

POSIX time has a resolution of no more than one second. A finer timestamp is recommended when message validity times are below 1 second, for example with fast moving routers.
sections.eli5: A note is only good for a short time. The time limit has to be long enough for the note to reach everyone, but not so long that an old note still works.

sections.title: Attacks Stopped and Limits
sections.content:
Because only routers holding the shared key can add a valid ICV, identity spoofing and link spoofing by outsiders are countered. With a shared key the receiver can tell a message came from a valid router but not which one, so a compromised router with valid keys can still impersonate another.

Replay attacks are only partly countered and depend on synchronized clocks. A recorded message can be replayed only within the allowed time window, and the attacker cannot change the protected timestamp. Inside the window replay is still possible, though the limits are chosen to keep its effect small.

If no synchronized clocks exist, replay cannot be countered. A timestamp variant with a monotonic sequence number may help partially but requires keeping state. Keys must be distributed out of band, and the RFC points to Section 23.6 of RFC 7181 for why automated key management does not apply here.
sections.eli5: Outsiders cannot fake the seal, and old notes expire. But a teammate who has gone bad still has the seal, and if clocks disagree, old notes cannot be caught.

layers.detail: Adds and checks ICV and TIMESTAMP TLVs; failed messages are dropped
